It's September 2031. Today “Ingrids Leseecke” (Ingrid's Reading Corner) opens at number 33. But outside there's a storm. Michael and Lena are getting the room ready.
Have you seen the weather forecast? Because of the storm, all outdoor events are apparently being cancelled today.
Luckily we're indoors. Despite the weather, thirty people have already confirmed.
Thirty? In this small room? Instead of a buffet, maybe we should just offer cake.
The cake is coming from my café. Andrei baked all night. In six hours he made five trays of apple cake.
And the books? Are all the shelves full?
Thanks to donations from the neighbourhood we have over eight hundred books. Mrs Schulze alone brought two crates.
Wonderful. And Mr Brandt? Is he coming despite his knee?
Of course! He's the guest of honour. He even wants to give a speech. He's been practising for a week while walking Fritz.
I have a surprise too. But I'll only reveal it during the party.
Nobody outside this room will find out anything, I promise. What is it?
No, no. Because of your curiosity I'm not revealing anything at all. You'll see at six.
“dess RAY-gens”: the final -s is clearly heard.
A few common prepositions take the genitive, especially in the written language:
because of, on the basis of
Masculine and neuter nouns take -s or -es: des Regens, des Knies, des Hauses, des Buches.
Possessives follow the indefinite article: wegen meines Bruders, trotz seiner Krankheit, während unserer Reise.

In everyday speech, many Germans use the dative after wegen, trotz, statt: “wegen dem Regen”, “trotz dem Wetter”. It's perfectly understood, but in writing, in exams and in formal situations use the genitive.
With “wegen” + pronoun there are special forms: meinetwegen (because of me / I don't mind), deinetwegen, seinetwegen. “Meinetwegen!” = Fine by me, I don't mind.
Without an article, in the plural, you switch to the dative to make it clear: “innerhalb von zwei Tagen”, “wegen Problemen”.
The constructions with a preposition are shorter and more elegant, typical of written texts and of B2 level.
Instead of a buffet, there was cake.
Thanks to the donations, we have 800 books.
Within a week everything was ready.
„Weil es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.” =
Trotz des Regens bleiben wir zu Hause.
Während des Regens bleiben wir zu Hause.

At five it started to rain, at half past five the storm broke. The wind tore the leaves off the chestnut trees and chased them down the street, and the rain beat so hard against the windows that you could barely hear your own words. Despite the bad weather, the guests came. They came with umbrellas blown inside out, with wet hair and wet shoes, and they were laughing as they stepped into the small, warm room on the ground floor of number thirty-three.

The room was unrecognisable. Where the coal cellar had once been, dark and damp, there were now light wooden shelves up to the ceiling, full of books. In the corner there were big soft cushions on the floor, for the children. By the window stood an old armchair with a reading lamp. And on the wall hung a photograph that Lena had chosen from Ludwig's album: Ingrid, at about forty, in her classroom, with a book in her hand and a laugh on her face.

They were all there. The Yilmaz family with their three children, freshly washed and in their best clothes. Mrs Schulze, who was given a seat right next to the photograph. Klaus, who was wearing a tie for the first time in years. Mara and Jakob, Kuba and Ola, Andrei with five trays of apple cake. Even Mrs Becker from the kiosk had come, with a bag full of old magazines as a donation, and she was unusually quiet for the first half hour.

Kuba and Ola immediately ran to the shelves and looked for the children's books. Ola found an old book of fairy tales with colourful illustrations, Kuba a thick novel about pirates. The three Yilmaz children stood shyly by the door at first, until Ola took them by the hand and led them to the cushions. Within ten minutes, five children were sitting together on the floor leafing through books, as if they had known each other for years. Michael watched them from the doorway, and Lena saw that he had tears in his eyes.

At six o'clock Michael tapped a glass and it went quiet. Ludwig stood up, leaning on his walking stick. In his hand he had a sheet of paper on which he had written down his speech. He put on his glasses, cleared his throat and began: “Dear neighbours, dear friends. When Michael asked me whether I wanted to say something today…”

At that moment lightning struck outside, so loudly that the children screamed, and the lights went out. Everywhere. In the room, on the stairs, in the whole street. A power cut. For a moment it was completely dark and silent, only the rain beat against the window. Then Mr Yilmaz's voice was heard: “No panic. I'm a bus driver. I always carry a torch.”

And then something lovely happened. Instead of a lamp, Lena lit the candles she had actually brought for the cakes. Mrs Schulze took two tea lights out of her handbag, “just in case, I learned that in the war”. Andrei found ten more candles in the café next door. Within five minutes the room was full of flickering little lights, and the books on the shelves cast long shadows on the ceiling. Suddenly it was very cosy.

“Like in the old days,” Mrs Schulze said quietly, and everyone looked at her. “During the war we often had no electricity. Then my mother would read aloud to us by candlelight, in the cellar, while the bombs were falling outside. I was two. I don't remember a single house that was destroyed back then. But I remember every story she read to us.” It was quiet in the room. Then Mr Yilmaz said: “Then let it be like that today too. Mr Brandt, please. Your speech.”
Well then. I can't read the sheet any more because of the darkness. Then I'll have to speak freely. Ingrid would have liked that. She always said the best speeches are the ones you haven't prepared.

And Ludwig spoke. He spoke about Ingrid, who for forty years had taught children to read, despite overcrowded classes, despite bad books, despite a state that prescribed what children were allowed to read. He spoke about a little boy on a staircase. He spoke about how a book is sometimes a door that you only have to open once. He spoke for ten minutes and nobody moved, not even the children.

At the end he said: “I'm not a teacher. For forty years I drove trams. But I lived next to a teacher and I learned one thing: because of a single book a whole life can change. Despite everything that has happened in this city, despite the war and the Wall and everything else, people like Ingrid and like Mrs Schulze's mother went on reading aloud. This room is for them. And for you, children. Open the doors.” Then he sat down and it was silent for a long time, until someone began to clap.

Then it was Michael's turn. “I promised you a surprise,” he said. “Here it is.” He opened the door, and in came, with a wet umbrella and a nervous smile, a small woman with short white hair, about seventy. Ludwig looked at her and needed only a second. “Renate,” he said. “Renate Kühn. The mother of the boy on the stairs.”

Mr Brandt. I never thanked you. Back then I worked twelve hours a day, at a laundry outside the city. I came home every evening and my son had eaten, had done his homework and could suddenly read. Thanks to your wife. And I was ashamed, because I hadn't managed it on my own. That's why I moved away without saying goodbye. I've been sorry for thirty years.

Ludwig walked slowly over to her, between the cushions and the children, and took both her hands. “Renate,” he said, “Ingrid never said anything other than: that woman is the bravest in the whole building. She works for two. We just help a little.” Renate cried, and Ludwig held her hands, in the light of thirty candles, beneath the photograph of a woman neither of them had forgotten.

After that, as he had promised, Michael read aloud the first chapter of «Emil und die Detektive», and the children sat on the cushions and listened open-mouthed. Then Kuba read a chapter, then Ola, who didn't dare at first and then read so well that everyone clapped. And then, right at the end, the youngest Yilmaz child, little seven-year-old Elif, took a picture book from the shelf, sat down in the big armchair by the window and read the first page aloud, slowly, word by word, with her finger under the letters. Nobody helped her. Everyone waited. And when she had finished, Mrs Becker was the first to clap.

The power only came back at ten. But by then nobody missed the lamps any more. While the last guests were putting on their wet coats, Ludwig was the last to blow out the candle beneath Ingrid's photograph and quietly said something that only Fritz heard.

On the way home, under Andrei's big umbrella, Lena asked him what he had said. Ludwig smiled. “I said: You see, Ingrid? Despite the storm. Because of the storm, maybe. It was the most beautiful evening in years.” Lena took his arm and they walked slowly up the wet Kastanienallee, past number thirty-three, where behind the ground-floor window a single candle was still burning.
